title: Play Sa-Re-Ga on a hand-pumped harmonium: one hand pumps the bellows nonstop while the other holds each key
instruction: Play the three marked keys on the harmonium in order, Sa (yellow dot), Re (green dot), Ga (blue dot), each held down for at least 4 seconds, going from one to the next without a gap in the sound. Pump the bellows at the back with your other hand the whole time so that the notes never die away. Then let go of the keys and the bellows.
context: A hand-pumped harmonium needs two simultaneous actions: one hand supplies air while the other plays the keys. The bellows board moves about 30 mm shut against about 12 N. A full reservoir sounds one key for about 3 s (under 3.1 s), so each four-second note needs pumping during the hold and the changes between notes. Neither hand alone can score: without air no reed sounds, and without a key no note sounds. Unlike TK-DPZS6F, which tests two-handed keyboard dynamics, this task combines continuous mechanical power with legato key control.
setup: Units mm; x forward from the line through the two arm bases, y to the robot's left, z up from the table top. Two YAM arms with parallel grippers (pads 94 apart when open), bases at (0, +305) and (0, -305), ready pose, grippers open; one overhead camera and one camera on each wrist (320 x 176). Wooden table top. 1) A standard Indian harmonium: 39 keys, 3 1/4 octaves (C2 to D5), 7 stops, double bellows, double reeds (for example the Banjira Standard 7-knob; listings give 559 x 305 x 254 with the lid and about 8 kg), teak-coloured wooden case, its lid off for playing so that the case is 205 tall, standing on its four rubber feet with the keyboard toward the robot, its front edge along x = 140 and centred on y = 0. The main stop (second from the left) is pulled out 20, the drones are closed. White keys 22 apart, 100 long, tops 180 above the table; a key goes down 7 against a spring (about 0.7 to 1.4 N) and its reed can speak once it is 2.5 down. Coloured dot stickers, 9 across, on Sa (C4, yellow), Re (D4, green) and Ga (E4, blue), whose centres are at y = -66, -88 and -110. The bellows board at the back is a 12 thick wooden board 530 wide and 189 tall, hinged along its bottom edge at x = 433, z = 16; its spring holds the top edge open at x = 500, z = 193; pushing it shut (to x = 445) takes about 12 N at the top edge and feeds the reservoir inside the case, which holds about 1.2 litres, enough for one held key for about 3 s. The reservoir starts empty. 2) Real trial only, not simulated: a microphone (a phone or USB microphone) on a 150 tall stand on the table at (600, -380), pointing at the harmonium. Nothing else is on the table. The layout is the same in every trial, as in the screenshot.
scoring: A real trial is judged from the microphone recording with a fixed, calibrated pitch rule, so no sound-level meter is needed. Calibration, just before the trial with the same instrument, microphone and room: a person pumps steadily and holds every key from C2 to D5 (all 39) for 1.5 s in turn, 0.5 s apart, then the room is recorded for 3 s with the robot powered and still (about 81 s in all). In 0.256 s analysis windows every 50 ms, a key's level is the sound power within 30 cents of its fundamental; its reference level is its median during its own calibration note. A key sounds in a 50 ms frame when its level is within 15 dB of its reference and at least 10 dB above that band's level in the silent recording (a knock, or a key pressed with the bellows empty, makes no reed tone and does not count). Overtones are not keys: taking the candidate keys in order of how close each is to its own reference, a key counts only if it is also at least 5 dB above what the keys already counted put into its band, as measured during their own calibration notes (C4's second harmonic falls on C5, a low key's fourth on C4); so a marked note never shows as a stray key and a stray low key never shows as Sa, Re or Ga, while any of the 39 keys really pressed is heard. Because those windows blur note edges by about 0.1 s, a frame whose own 50 ms of sound has its 200 to 2,000 Hz band more than 20 dB below the median of the calibration notes counts as silent, so a break between notes is timed to within 50 ms. Also measure once how long one held key sounds after pumping stops with the reservoir full: the hold time H below is 4.0 s, or that time plus 1 s if longer. A note is held when it sounds continuously for at least H, gaps of 0.1 s or less bridged. 0.25: Sa held. 0.5: Sa held, then Re held (Re starts and ends after Sa). 0.75: Sa, Re and Ga held in that order. 0.85: in addition each change of note leaves at most 0.5 s of silence and overlaps the previous note by at most 1.0 s (longer is a chord), no other key sounds for more than 0.2 s in total, the harmonium never moves more than 10 mm from its marks, and at the end both grippers are off the harmonium (keys, bellows board and case) with every key up for at least 1 s. 1.0: all that, and the sound never breaks: each next note starts before the previous one stops (legato, as players do it) or at most 0.1 s (two frames) after. The score is 0 if the harmonium is ever pushed more than 30 mm from its marks or tipped more than 5 degrees. In simulation the same rules run on the simulator's sounding keys, read every 50 ms: a key's reed sounds while that key is at least 2.5 mm down and the reservoir pressure (from the air rule) is above the reed's speaking pressure. The trial ends at the run limit, or once the score is 1.0. Possible scores: 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 0.85, 1.0.
reset_notes: Push the stops back except the main stop (pulled out 20 mm), close the drones, let the bellows board spring open and let the reservoir run empty (hold a key until it falls silent). Stand the harmonium back on its tape marks. Return both arms to ready with grippers open. Nothing is consumed. In simulation: seed 0, no jitter; the harmonium is put back on its marks with its board open, keys up and reservoir empty, and the scorer starts fresh.
fidelity: Isaac Lab-Arena rigid bodies at listed size and mass; 240 Hz physics, 20 Hz control. The case, all 39 keys and bellows board move through contact, with no loop joints or gripper attachments. Air is a rule: constant 2.19 N m at 200 Pa; swept feed (9.5 L) into a 1.2 L reservoir at 160 to 230 Pa; each reed uses about 0.4 L/s. Sound and bellows folds are synthesized. Forces, flow and spring rates are estimates. See TECHNICAL.md for details and real-audio scoring.
scores: Dream-1 run: 0.0 (2,400 steps; it moved both grippers, mostly closed, over the harmonium, pressed on the top of the case and pushed two black keys (F#3, A#3) part way down, but never touched the bellows board, so no air went in and no note sounded); demo: 1.0 (464 steps). Both runs on the final package files.
